A verity is a truth — but a very specific kind of truth. It is a truth that is deep, fundamental, and lasting. Not a passing observation, not a personal opinion, not a temporary fact — but a truth so solid and timeless that it holds firm across centuries, cultures, and circumstances.

Think of it this way: if you say "it rained yesterday," that is a fact. If you say "I think honesty matters," that is an opinion. But if you say "human beings need love to thrive" — that is the kind of truth a verity points to. Something foundational. Something that has always been true and will always be true.

The word "verity" is used in two related but slightly different ways:

1. A specific fundamental truth (the most common use)
Here, "a verity" or "the verities" refers to a particular truth — usually a deep moral, philosophical, or spiritual one. It is almost always used for truths about the human condition, about life and existence, about what is right or just.

  • "That all living things must die is one of life's great verities."
  • "The poem returns to the eternal verities — love, loss, and the passage of time."

2. The quality of being true (less common, more abstract)
Sometimes "verity" is used more broadly to mean the state or quality of something being true — its truthfulness or reality.

  • "No one doubted the verity of his account."

(Meaning: no one doubted that his account was true, that it was the real truth.)

In practice, you will encounter the first sense far more often.

These three words are related, but they are not interchangeable. Here is the key difference:

  • A fact is specific and verifiable. "The Earth orbits the Sun." It is true, but it is narrow.
  • A truth is broader. It can be personal, general, or even subjective. "It's the truth that he never loved her."
  • A verity is grander and more timeless than either. It refers to a truth of deep, enduring significance — usually one that speaks to human nature, morality, or existence itself. "That cruelty destroys the soul of the one who practices it is an ancient verity."

You would not call a weather report a verity. You would not call a shopping receipt a verity. The word naturally belongs in conversation about things that are big, timeless, and morally or philosophically weighty.
The Word Has a Sense of Authority and Weight

When someone calls something a verity, they are saying: "This is not up for debate. This is not a trend or a theory. This is a deep truth that has stood the test of time." The word carries a sense of solemnity, gravity, and conviction.

It is the kind of word used by philosophers, theologians, poets, essayists, and thinkers — people wrestling with serious ideas about life and what it means to be human.

The plural form, verities, is extremely common — often even more common than the singular. Writers and thinkers frequently speak of "the verities" as a group, referring collectively to the core truths of human life.

The most famous phrase associated with this word is "the eternal verities" — a phrase used to describe the permanent, universal truths of human existence. Things like: the reality of death, the power of love, the need for justice, the inevitability of suffering, the beauty of goodness. These are the eternal verities — the deep truths that every human being across all of history has had to face.

  • "Great literature always returns to the eternal verities."
  • "He had lived long enough to know which verities actually mattered."
  • "Beneath all the noise of modern life, the old verities remain unchanged."
The Register: A Formal, Literary Word

"Verity" is not a word you would use in casual conversation. It belongs to a formal, literary, or philosophical register. You are far more likely to read it in:

  • Essays and academic writing
  • Philosophy and theology
  • Literary fiction and poetry
  • Speeches and formal addresses
  • Serious journalism or cultural commentary

If you used it in everyday speech ("Oh, that's definitely a verity"), it would sound unusual or even slightly theatrical. That is not a flaw in the word — it simply means it has a specific, elevated home.

One Final Way to Cement It

Imagine a very old, very wise person at the end of their life, speaking slowly and with great weight, sharing the most important things they have learned. The things they say in that moment — the deep, irreducible truths about love, loss, courage, kindness, and mortality — those are verities. Not opinions. Not preferences. Not trends. The real, lasting stuff underneath everything.

That is what "verity" reaches for every time it is used.
